correctness.rationale: The proof separates domination from complement connectivity. Domination is exhaustive by the two bipartition occupancies. Every nonempty induced complement is either one-sided or is a complete bipartite graph with a matching deleted; the only disconnected mixed cases are a matched singleton side and the two-by-two full matching deletion. Inclusion-exclusion over those obstruction classes gives the displayed polynomial. The minimum transition follows because deleting a matched pair leaves the crown graph of one smaller index. The packaged exhaustive checker independently matches every coefficient for n from three through eight.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The primary polynomial paper covers the minimum parameter on complete multipartite graphs and coefficient formulas for several other families; the algorithmic paper gives a chain-graph algorithm. Crown graphs with n at least three are neither complete multipartite nor chain graphs, so neither broader statement specializes to this family.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The known complete-multipartite value gives only a lower bound through spanning-subgraph monotonicity. It does not force equality after deleting a perfect matching: at n equals three the crown value rises from two to four. Thus even the minimum transition is not a corollary of the complete-bipartite value, and the coefficientwise polynomial is strictly stronger information.

value.rationale: The crown graph is a standard near-complete bipartite family, and outer-connected domination is sensitive to the connectivity of the omitted set rather than only to domination. The result classifies every feasible set, gives the full polynomial and total count, and exposes a genuine edge-deletion threshold: the natural two-vertex dominating pairs fail exactly at the first connected crown. This is a structural enumeration rather than a single routine parameter evaluation.
